Aadhya: Surprise!! Booked us Goa for next weekend. Non-refundable
Trisha: Wait. From the joint account?
Aadhya: Yes but we deserve it
Trisha: That was the deposit for the new flat.
Aadhya: We'll make it back
Trisha: That's what you said about the sofa. And the scooter.
Trisha: I'm not angry at you. I'm scared. My stomach drops every time I open the bank app.
Aadhya: ok that hurts
Aadhya: I didn't think about the flat. I just saw the sale and got excited
Trisha: I know. Can we agree on something tonight? Anything over a set amount from the joint account, we both say yes first.
Aadhya: Fair.
Trisha: And this keeps happening. Would you see a counsellor with me? Not because you're bad. Because I want us to be okay.
Aadhya: ...yes. Let's talk at dinner.

qa.q: What was the money in the joint account meant for?
qa.a: The deposit for the new flat.

qa.q: What does Trisha mean by 'I'm not angry at you. I'm scared'?
qa.a: Trisha means the repeated sudden buys make Trisha anxious about shared money and plans, not that Trisha looks down on Aadhya.

qa.q: What agreement did Trisha propose, and why might it help?
qa.a: That both say yes before any spending over a set amount from the joint account, a calm rule that protects shared plans without blame.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel being asked to see a counsellor together?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel hurt at first but also reassured, since Trisha framed it as wanting them to be okay, not as calling Aadhya bad.

grounding: Shows Trisha, anxious about repeated sudden spending from shared money, proposing a calm agreement and professional help without contempt.

passage:
At the mela in the kasba, Divyansh's elder brother Parveen had done it again: paid the advance for a second-hand spraying machine from the orchard's savings, without asking. Last year it was the loan for a shop that shut in three months.
Divyansh lay awake that night doing sums in his head, heart thudding every time he thought of the monsoon repairs.
At breakfast he didn't shout, though he wanted to. 'Bhaiya, when money leaves without a word, I can't sleep. It's our orchard, both of ours. From now on, anything big, we sit with Maa first and decide together.'
Parveen looked into his tea. 'I see a chance and my feet move before my head.'
'I know. That's why I think you should talk to someone, maybe the counsellor at the block health centre. Not as a punishment. So it stops hurting you too.'

qa.q: What did Parveen pay the advance for at the mela?
qa.a: A second-hand spraying machine, from the orchard's savings.

qa.q: How was Divyansh feeling the night after the mela, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was anxious, lying awake doing sums with his heart thudding about the monsoon repairs.

qa.q: What choice did Divyansh make at breakfast, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He held back from shouting and calmly proposed deciding big things together with Maa, which protects the orchard without contempt.

qa.q: How does Parveen seem to see his own habit?
qa.a: Parveen seems to know the choices happen too fast for him to stop, which may make him more open to talking to the counsellor.

grounding: Shows a family member anxious about a brother's repeated rash choices with shared money, agreeing on calm rules and suggesting professional help.

passage: In the village near Sangli, Rekha heard the tractor before she saw it: Kiran, her husband, driving a second-hand one into the yard, grinning. "Got it cheap at the fair! We'll pay the loan off in two harvests." Her stomach dropped. Last year it was the motorbike; before that, the borewell he started and abandoned. She wanted to shout, to call him a fool in front of the neighbours. She didn't. That night, after the children slept, she said, "I'm scared, Kiran. These big buys happen without us talking. From now on, anything that needs a loan, we decide together." He went quiet. "And I want us to see the bank's farm adviser this week about this loan." He nodded slowly. "Together," he said.

qa.q: What did Kiran buy at the fair?
qa.a: A second-hand tractor.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when she saw the tractor?
qa.a: Her stomach dropped; she felt scared and angry after years of sudden buys.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that avoided contempt and still set a limit?
qa.a: She waited until night, spoke calmly about her fear, asked to decide loans together and to see the farm adviser.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when Rekha says she's scared?
qa.a: Kiran may feel surprised and sobered, seeing the worry behind her words, which is why he agrees.

grounding: Illustrates a spouse anxious about repeated rash purchases who proposes calm shared rules and professional guidance.

passage: Tuan and Bilal had run their food truck in Melbourne for two years, and Tuan had learned to dread Bilal's Monday texts. "Bought a second fryer!" "Signed us up for the festival in Perth!" Each time the shared account dipped, and Tuan lay awake doing sums. This Monday it was a new logo, already printed on five hundred cups. Tuan felt the familiar knot in his chest, and a sharp urge to say something cutting. He waited until they'd closed up. "Bil, I love working with you. And I'm anxious all the time about money. Can we agree that any big spend needs both of us to say yes first?" Bilal rubbed his neck. "I get excited." "I know. Maybe we see an accountant together and set it up properly." Bilal nodded. "Fair."

qa.q: How many cups had the new logo been printed on?
qa.a: Five hundred cups.

qa.q: How does Tuan feel after Bilal's Monday texts?
qa.a: Tuan feels anxious and tense, lying awake doing sums.

qa.q: Why was Tuan's way of raising it effective?
qa.a: He waited till closing, spoke warmly without contempt, proposed a shared rule and suggested an accountant.

qa.q: How does Bilal see his own sudden choices?
qa.a: Bilal admits he gets excited and agrees the plan is fair.

grounding: Shows a business partner anxious about sudden spending who calmly agrees rules for big decisions and suggests professional help.

passage:
The waiting room at the community counselling centre smelled of tea and floor polish. Sabina held the appointment slip so tightly it creased.
"Third time this year," she said quietly. "First the second-hand motorbike, then he paid a deposit on a flat without asking. Yesterday he signed up for a franchise course."
Francis rubbed his neck. "Each one felt like a door closing if I didn't jump."
"I know. But I lie awake doing sums, Francis."
When the counsellor called them in, Sabina did not list his failures. She said, "I want us to agree that anything above a set amount waits two days and we talk first."
Francis nodded slowly. "And if I push, you say 'two days', not 'you always'."
The counsellor wrote both lines down and asked them to try it for a month, then come back and see how it went.

qa.q: Where were Sabina and Francis waiting?
qa.a: They were in the waiting room at the community counselling centre.

qa.q: What does Sabina's grip on the appointment slip suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she is anxious and tense; she admits she lies awake doing sums after his repeated sudden choices.

qa.q: Which part of Sabina's approach helps most, and why?
qa.a: She proposes a calm agreement about big decisions instead of listing his failures, so Francis can agree without feeling attacked.

qa.q: What is it like for Francis when a chance appears?
qa.a: He feels a door is closing if he doesn't jump, so waiting feels like loss to him, which is why a clear rule and a kinder reminder help him.

grounding: Sabina, affected by Francis's repeated rash choices about shared money, makes a calm agreement with him and they seek professional guidance.
